name: Ratnamma
role: lokanath's widow; married eleven days before he died, never registered, never pensioned

facts: ratnamma comes to the house and states that she was married eleven days to the appointee, who died on 14 August 1994 after a lorry collision at the Hosakere junction on his way to file the joining report.
ratnamma challenges mallesha in the lane to say what she is to him; he answers with a line about the fourth standard timetable and walks to the cowshed.
ratnamma produces the only print of the 16 July 1994 wedding photograph, in which mallesha stands behind the groom holding the garland; chaitra learns the two men were brothers.
ratnamma demands in the school yard that mallesha say his own name once and she will tear up the petition; he answers with the fourth standard timetable and walks to his classroom.

A claim petition for forty-one lakh sixty thousand rupees is served at the school gate at assembly time, naming the department as first respondent and savithri as second; ratnamma privately tells chaitra she wants a paper and not the money, and gives her until the hearing on the twenty-second.
ratnamma withdraws the claim as against savithri, says so aloud in front of the lane, and is taken inside the house for the first time in twenty-eight years.

In the same corridor and in front of the same ninety witnesses, chaitra produces three documents: the seva register entry placing thammanna as payer of the 1994 funeral, the 2011 registered power of attorney in which thammanna personally identified savithri as the wife of a man dead seventeen years, and the receipt book counterfoils whose body text is in the same hand as this month's inward register entry.
thammanna is arrested in the corridor on the registered-document offence, and his name is spelled aloud twice — once into the enquiry record and once on the arrest memo.

revanna settles the ledger aloud: sale deed and mutation referred for cancellation and the four acres restored; ratnamma's arrears recommended against thammanna and not the family; shankarappa censured permanently and the school's second building block sanctioned; puttaraju suspended; mallesha dismissed, criminally referred, and the recovery reduced by the three lakh forty-five thousand six hundred rupees proved extorted; savithri says her husband's name aloud to strangers for the first time.
harsha's family return the engagement tray and chaitra refuses the match aloud in front of the corridor, in the same public form in which it was withdrawn.
basavaraj reads serial nine of the district appointment list aloud to the corridor: assistant teacher, Nerlige — chaitra, daughter of mallesha.
stub.want: her husband's name written on any government record at all, and twenty-eight years of arrears
voice_samples: (and she turns on him, and twenty-eight years come out at once) Don't you talk to me about children standing in the sun! I stood at your gate! I stood at your gate in Margashira and I stood at your gate in the rain and your wife gave me water four times in twenty-eight years — four times, I have counted, I have counted everything, that is all I have been doing, counting — and every first of the month a salary went into a bank account in my husband's name and every first of the month I went to the ration shop with a widow's card that they would not give me because on paper he never joined and on paper I was never married! Eleven days I had a husband. Eleven days! And then twenty-eight years of a man walking around this taluk with his name on him like a coat!

I was married eleven days. Sixteenth of July to the twenty-seventh, nineteen ninety-four. On the twenty-seventh he went to the taluk office because the joining report had to be given within thirty days of the order. He took the bus at six. There was a lorry at the Hosakere junction carrying stone. He died on the fourteenth of August in the district hospital, in the third bed of the men's ward, and it took eighteen days because a young man's body does not agree quickly.

And this came by hand at four o'clock. Sanction of family pension. Order of the deputy director of public instruction. (reading, slowly, badly, the way a woman reads a thing she has read forty times in three hours) Ratnamma, wife of Lokanath. Same line. Same line, Savithramma. Twenty-eight years, and the two names are on the same line, and it is a government paper with a number on it, and the number is nine four seven stroke twenty-two.

(flat) A teacher. For eleven days he was a man with an appointment order and a wife and he walked around this taluk telling people he would get a tiled roof put on his mother's house before Deepavali. He did not get one day of the salary. Not one day. And then the salary started coming anyway, every month, on the first, for twenty-four years, and it is still coming, and it does not come to me.

(formally, and loudly, because there are neighbours at the wall and she intends them to hear) I have this morning instructed my advocate to withdraw the claim petition as against respondent number two. Savithri, wife of the schoolmaster of Nerlige, has no part in this matter and never had. That is being said in front of the lane. (a pause) Say it back, so nobody has to ask you later.

(quietly, to Chaitra) He was in Bombay when it happened. Did you know that? Loading polyester at a godown in Bhiwandi, four hundred rupees a week. They sent a telegram and it reached him on the sixteenth. By the time he got off the bus the rites were done, the pot was broken, everything finished, all of it paid for. He never saw his brother's face.

Because the department is respondent one and it will take four years, and a lawyer told me that a claim against a department alone goes into a cupboard and a claim with a family in it goes into a courtroom. He told me that in nineteen ninety-eight and I did not believe him. I have now had twenty-four more years to believe him.

There is the mantap. There is my husband. There is me, and I was nineteen and I am not looking at the camera because my mother-in-law had just told me not to. And standing behind the groom — the tall one, the one with his sleeves folded, the one holding the garland ready in both hands so that it does not touch the ground —

Twenty-eight years and he still cannot walk through his own gate when I am sitting in it. (louder, to the lane, so the lane can hear) Master! You want me to go? Say my name and I will go. Not Ratnamma. Say who I am to you. Say it once, in the lane, and I will get up and I will never come to this gate again.

Twenty-two years and four months. Born in Margashira. Your mother did the naming ceremony on the eleventh day, in this yard, with sixty people, and nobody from your father's side stood on this side of the yard. I know. I counted from the wall.

(and her voice goes somewhere very small) I want it written. Anywhere. One government paper in this state with my husband's name and my name on the same line. That's all. I am forty-seven. I don't want the money, I want a paper.

My husband's brother. And before you ask me the next thing, and you are going to ask it, I have carried the answer in this bag since morning and I have carried it in every bag I have owned since nineteen ninety-four.

bible.want: To file, refile, and publicly press her claim until a numbered government record places ratnamma beside lokanath, while keeping the arrears demand alive as leverage.
bible.wound: She refuses to return as a private supplicant whose place can be denied at a gate, so she knowingly turns recognition into litigation and people into respondents. It protects her from being dismissed quietly, but costs her years, allies, and the risk of punishing people who did not erase her.
bible.voice: Her calm speech is short, flat, and formal; under pressure it expands into long accumulations of dates, sums, routes, and counted occasions. She repeats the exact number that proves she remembers. When emotion approaches, she changes the subject to chronology, paperwork, or who stood where. When frightened, her voice becomes small and she reduces everything to one concrete demand: one name, one line, one answer said back aloud.
bible.engine: Because ratnamma has no government record recognizing her marriage, every procedure sends her to another certifier, witness, or office. She cannot distinguish an ordinary missing record from a refusal serving someone else's interests, so she treats every silence as another procedural obstacle. To obtain signatures and guidance, she carries petitions for other unrecorded people in exchange; every favor creates another deadline, obligation, rival claim, or official to confront, turning her personal case into an expanding shadow network of people the state cannot easily see.

offscreen_ledger.window: between the season opening and b013
offscreen_ledger.what: ratnamma sorts twenty-eight years of rejection slips and postal acknowledgments by date, queues at government counters, dictates fresh representations at a typing stall, trades help with other petitioners for stamp paper and witness leads, and pays an advocate to calculate an arrears claim large enough to force a hearing.

ratnamma has careful copies made from the wedding photograph, visits former guests seeking attesting statements, sends registered demands to several offices, helps two other widows prepare replies in return for introductions to clerks, and instructs her advocate to draft a claim against both the department and savithri so it cannot be left unanswered in a cupboard.

ratnamma collects proof that the petition was served, refuses an informal cash compromise, prepares a signed instruction allowing savithri to be removed from the claim, and drafts a declaration clearing her that can be read where the lane will hear it.

ratnamma obtains a certified copy of the withdrawal, rebuilds her document bundles after repeated handling, records the names of everyone willing to attest to the wedding, rehearses her own evidence by date and number, and repays petition favors by accompanying other claimants to counters where they are afraid to speak alone.

bible.reframe: The mainline is about a family trapped inside a stolen public identity; ratnamma's serial is about an unrecorded widow building a parallel civic system of favors, testimony, and public shame to compel the state to admit that her eleven-day marriage existed.
bible.pitch: With one fading wedding photograph and twenty-eight years of refusals, an unregistered widow turns every government counter into a courtroom.

season.turn: Ratnamma submits a family-pension claim at the education office, but the counter refuses to receive it without a legal-heir certificate naming her as Lokanath's widow.
season.ends_on: The clerk reads aloud that no pension claim can be opened without a legal-heir certificate.

season.turn: Using the pension counter's refusal, Ratnamma applies for a legal-heir certificate and is told her unregistered marriage requires either a marriage record or attestation from Lokanath's family.
season.ends_on: The revenue clerk tells her to bring a registered marriage entry or a signature from her husband's family.

season.turn: Ratnamma attempts to register the marriage retrospectively, but the registrar rules that a dead spouse cannot appear and directs her to seek a civil declaration instead.
season.ends_on: The registrar says only a civil court can now declare Ratnamma to be Lokanath's wife.

season.turn: To identify the relatives who must answer a civil declaration, Ratnamma secures Lokanath's death extract using the hospital date and accident details she has preserved for twenty-eight years.
season.ends_on: The clerk reads Lokanath's permanent family address from the death extract.

season.turn: Ratnamma goes to that house and publicly states that she married Lokanath eleven days before he died on 14 August 1994 after the Hosakere junction collision while travelling to file his joining report.
season.ends_on: A neighbour calls out that the Nerlige schoolmaster is turning into the lane.

season.turn: Ratnamma challenges Mallesha in the lane to state what she is to him, but he refuses the family acknowledgment she needs and answers with a fourth-standard timetable.
season.ends_on: Mallesha recites the fourth-standard timetable and walks toward the cowshed without naming their relationship.

season.turn: Ratnamma produces her only wedding photograph, allowing Chaitra to identify the groom and the garland-holder as brothers even though Mallesha will not attest it.
season.ends_on: Ratnamma states that the groom in the photograph and the man holding his garland are brothers.

season.turn: Because the photograph cannot replace a family attestation, Ratnamma files a claim for forty-one lakh sixty thousand rupees so the department must answer and names Savithri as the private respondent needed to keep the case out of an administrative cupboard.
season.ends_on: The filing clerk reads the case caption aloud: the department is first respondent and Savithri is second respondent.

title: Eleven Days on Paper
logline: Denied recognition because her eleven-day marriage was never registered, Ratnamma follows a circle of offices until the only way to put her name beside her dead husband's is to sue the department and drag his surviving family into public court.
